summary: Summarizes research on how the DNS is deployed and configured, and offers practical advice to operators of large authoritative DNS servers. Following the advice may improve their services. Some findings may also apply to other stateless, short-duration anycasted services. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Tips for people who run very busy DNS answer servers, based on studies of what works well.

questions: how to run a large dns service
how to run an authoritative dns server
subtitle: Research-backed advice for operating large DNS server networks

tldr.problem: Large authoritative DNS servers face challenges in deployment, latency optimization, and resilience to attacks, with no clear guidance on best practices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes six peer-reviewed research studies on DNS deployment and proposes specific operational considerations: anycast deployment, routing optimization, catchment mapping, stress strategies, TTL tuning, and parent-child TTL coordination.
tldr.outcome: Operators of large DNS services gain evidence-based guidance to reduce latency, handle distributed denial-of-service attacks, and improve reliability of their services.

today: RFC 9199 is an informational document that remains current guidance. It synthesizes peer-reviewed research through 2019 and provides practical advice to DNS operators worldwide.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document summarizes research on how large authoritative DNS servers are deployed and operated. An authoritative DNS server knows the answer to queries about a particular domain and serves that information to recursive resolvers worldwide. The RFC presents six research-backed considerations for operators who manage these large services, which typically serve many users globally and use anycast, a technique that announces the same IP address from multiple physical locations.

The considerations are based on measurements using the RIPE Atlas platform and case studies of real DNS operators, including studies of root DNS servers and major top-level domains. Rather than prescriptive rules, these are evidence-based engineering options that operators may choose to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains six smart ways to run a very busy DNS server that many people rely on. The ideas come from studying how the biggest DNS services actually work.

sections.title: Anycast Deployment and Routing Optimization
sections.content:
The first consideration is that authoritative DNS operators should deploy anycast for every server in their zone's NS records. Anycast allows the same IP address to be reachable from multiple geographic locations, and research shows that recursive resolvers query all available authoritative servers and distribute traffic towards the closest ones by latency. This means operators cannot rely on only some of their servers being deployed with anycast; all of them must provide good latency worldwide.

The second key finding is that optimizing routing policies matters more than simply adding more physical locations. A study comparing root DNS servers found that a server with only eight anycast instances provided similar latency to servers with 33 and 144 instances respectively. This is because proper interconnectivity and routing engineering can outweigh the sheer number of locations.
sections.plainLanguage: Put the same service in many places around the world so queries reach a nearby copy. Make sure your network routing is good—being smart about routing helps more than just building more locations.

sections.title: Anycast Catchment Mapping and Stress Handling
sections.content:
The third consideration is that operators should measure and map how traffic distributes across their anycast instances. A tool called Verfploeter can predict which remote networks will route to each anycast location before the operator deploys a new site, helping avoid overloading some locations while leaving others underutilized.

The fourth consideration addresses how operators should react when an anycast instance comes under attack or is overloaded. Research on the November 2015 DNS root denial-of-service event found that operators use two distinct strategies: either withdrawing or prepending routes to shift traffic to other instances, or deliberately absorbing attack traffic at the overloaded site to protect others. Operators should prepare both strategies in advance, documented in operational playbooks so they can be deployed rapidly.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you add a new location, measure where traffic will go to avoid surprises. When you're under attack, have two plans ready: send traffic elsewhere, or stay and protect the other locations.

sections.title: Time-to-Live Configuration
sections.content:
The fifth consideration concerns Time-to-Live (TTL) values, which control how long recursive resolvers cache DNS records. A measurement study that increased the TTL of a TLD from five minutes to one day found that median latency dropped from 28.7 ms to 8 ms as a result of better cache hits. Longer TTLs also reduce the load on authoritative servers and provide better protection against denial-of-service attacks because cached data survives short outages.

However, longer TTLs slow down the operator's ability to make rapid changes. The RFC recommends that general zones use TTLs of at least one hour, and that registry operators for large TLD zones also use longer TTLs. For services using DNS-based load balancing or DDoS mitigation, shorter TTLs of 5 to 15 minutes may be necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Longer expiry times on cached answers make things faster and protect against attacks, but they make it harder to change things quickly. Pick a balance that fits your needs.

sections.title: Parent-Child TTL Coordination
sections.content:
The sixth consideration addresses a subtle problem: when a parent zone and child zone publish different TTL values for the same record, different recursive resolvers honor different TTLs. A measurement study found that about 90 percent of resolvers follow the child's TTL, while 10 percent follow the parent's. For in-bailiwick authoritative servers (those inside the domain), the study found that most resolvers will requery for address records when the NS record TTL expires, even if the address records should still be valid.

Operators planning infrastructure changes should assume that both parent and child TTLs apply and keep old infrastructure operational for the maximum of the two values to ensure a smooth transition.
sections.plainLanguage: Parent and child zones sometimes have different expiry times. Assume both apply, and don't turn off old servers until enough time has passed for both to expire.
